clinician.final_diagnosis: CT angiography of the whole aorta revealed aortic thrombosis, extending from the level of the diaphragm to the aortic bifurcation
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 25-year-old man with Crohn's disease presented with sudden onset paraplegia, lower extremity pain, numbness, paralysis, and faecal incontinence, along with signs of lower limb ischemia (pale, cold, numb legs, flaccid paralysis, impalpable pulses). Initial labs showed metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and creatinine. CT angiography of the whole aorta confirmed the diagnosis of aortic thrombosis, extending from the diaphragm to the aortic bifurcation, with no signs of atherosclerosis. He underwent open exploration, thrombectomy, and stenting of the right renal artery, superior mesenteric artery, and distal aorta. Post-reperfusion, he developed massive leg swelling requiring fasciotomies and a second-look surgery where his gallbladder was removed. After 3.5 months of inpatient spinal rehabilitation, he regained some sensory function but remained wheelchair-dependent. Investigation for coagulation disorders was inconclusive, and the underlying cause of the thrombosis remained a mystery.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient presented with sudden onset paraplegia, lower extremity pain, numbness, paralysis, and faecal incontinence, along with signs of lower limb ischemia (pale, cold, numb legs, flaccid paralysis, impalpable pulses).
Initial labs showed metabolic acidosis (pH 7.2, base excess −13 mmol/L, lactate 6.2 mmol/L) and elevated creatinine (155 µmol/L).
CT angiography of the whole aorta revealed aortic thrombosis, extending from the level of the diaphragm to the aortic bifurcation, with no signs of atherosclerosis.

Surgical intervention included open exploration revealing extensive visceral ischemia, followed by endovascular thrombectomy and stenting of the right renal artery, superior mesenteric artery, and distal aorta.
Post-reperfusion, massive leg swelling required several fasciotomies, and a second-look surgery involved gallbladder removal.
After 3.5 months of inpatient spinal rehabilitation, the patient regained some sensory function but remained wheelchair-dependent.
